front: Opportunity cost per unit, read off a PPC or an output table.
cue: Comparative advantage and moving along a PPC.
formula: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>opportunity cost of 1 unit of X</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{opportunity cost of 1 unit of X}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>units of Y given up</mtext><mtext>units of X gained</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{units of Y given up}}{\text{units of X gained}}</annotation></semantics></math>
worked: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>20</mn><mtext> bolts</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn><mtext> chairs</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{20 \text{ bolts}}{10 \text{ chairs}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext> bolts per chair</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 2\,\text{ bolts per chair}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Comparative advantage goes to the lower opportunity cost, not the larger output (that is absolute advantage).

cue: Choosing the bundle that maximizes total utility: equal MU per dollar across goods, budget spent.
formula: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>marginal utility per dollar</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{marginal utility per dollar}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>U</mi></mrow><mi>P</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{MU}{P}</annotation></semantics></math>
worked: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>30</mn><mtext> utils</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo>$</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{30 \text{ utils}}{$2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>15</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext> utils per dollar</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 15\,\text{ utils per dollar}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Compare MU divided by price, not MU alone, and stop when the budget runs out.

cue: Every elasticity starts from two of them.
trap: Divide by the old value, and keep the sign until you take the absolute value.

cue: How strongly buyers respond to a price change; the total revenue test.
worked: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">|</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left| \frac{-20\%}{+10\%} \right| = 2</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Quantity on top, price on the bottom; read the absolute value: above 1 is elastic, below 1 inelastic.

front: The price elasticity of demand by the midpoint method.
cue: One route that gives the same answer whichever way the price moves (not keyed as the only route).
formula: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_d</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">|</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>/</mo><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>/</mo><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \left| \frac{(Q_2 - Q_1) / \tfrac{Q_1 + Q_2}{2}}{(P_2 - P_1) / \tfrac{P_1 + P_2}{2}} \right|</annotation></semantics></math>
worked: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">|</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>90</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left| \frac{-20 / 90}{+2 / 11} \right|</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>1.22</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 1.22</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Each change is divided by the average of the two values.

cue: Telling normal goods (positive) from inferior goods (negative).
trap: The sign matters here: keep it.

cue: Telling substitutes (positive) from complements (negative).
worked: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">+</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1.25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{-25\%}{+20\%} = -1.25</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Positive means substitutes, negative means complements; the price is the other good's.

cue: The total revenue test, and a firm's revenue at its output.
trap: With elastic demand a price cut raises total revenue; with inelastic demand it lowers it.

front: Consumer surplus under a straight demand curve.
cue: Surplus at equilibrium and after a change.
formula: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">CS</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>×</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>top of demand</mtext><mo>−</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \tfrac{1}{2} \times Q \times (\text{top of demand} - P)</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: A triangle needs the one half; use the quantity actually bought.

front: The government's revenue from a per-unit tax.
cue: Shading and sizing the tax rectangle.
formula: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>tax revenue</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{tax revenue}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>tax per unit</mtext><mo>×</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mtext>after</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{tax per unit} \times Q_{\text{after}}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Use the quantity after the tax, not the old equilibrium quantity.

front: What a per-unit subsidy costs the government.
cue: Shading and sizing the subsidy rectangle.
formula: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>subsidy cost</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{subsidy cost}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>subsidy per unit</mtext><mo>×</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mtext>after</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{subsidy per unit} \times Q_{\text{after}}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: The whole rectangle between the price sellers receive and the price buyers pay, out to the new, larger quantity.

cue: Taxes, subsidies, price controls, monopoly and externalities.
formula: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>W</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">DWL</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>×</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>×</mo><mtext>price wedge</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \tfrac{1}{2} \times \Delta Q \times \text{price wedge}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Between demand (MSB) and supply (MC, MSC), from the quantity traded to the efficient quantity; do not forget the one half.

front: A shortage at a binding price ceiling (a surplus is the reverse).
cue: Price controls.
trap: Quantity demanded against quantity supplied at the controlled price, not demand against supply.

front: The government's revenue from a tariff.
cue: A domestic market with a world price and a tariff.
trap: Imports after the tariff: quantity demanded minus quantity supplied at the higher price.

cue: A production table; diminishing marginal returns.
worked: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>25</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{25 - 15}{3 - 2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>10</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext> units</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 10\,\text{ units}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: The change in output from one more worker, not output per worker (that is average product).

cue: A cost table; the MR = MC rule.
trap: Divide the change in total cost by the change in output, which is not always 1.

front: Average total and average variable cost.
cue: A cost table; profit per unit; the shutdown point (minimum AVC).
trap: Divide by output, and remember TC = TFC + TVC.

cue: A cost table.
trap: Divide fixed cost by output, not by workers; TFC is the same at every output, including zero.

cue: Sizing the profit or loss rectangle.
formula: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>profit</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{profit}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= TR - TC</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>Q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= (P - ATC) \times Q</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Use ATC at the profit-maximizing quantity, and subtract implicit costs for economic profit.

front: Economic profit, against accounting profit (TR minus explicit costs only).
cue: An owner who gives up a salary or interest to run the business.
formula: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>economic profit</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{economic profit}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mtext>explicit</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>implicit costs</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= TR - \text{explicit} - \text{implicit costs}</annotation></semantics></math>
worked: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90{,}000 - 60{,}000 - 40{,}000</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext> dollars</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -10{,}000\,\text{ dollars}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Accounting profit is larger whenever implicit costs are positive.

front: Marginal revenue product (MP x P when the firm sells in a competitive product market).
cue: A hiring table; labor demand.
trap: Marginal product times marginal revenue, never MR times P.

cue: Hiring where MRP = MRC; a monopsony's MFC.
trap: For a firm that takes the market wage, MRC is the wage; for a monopsonist it is above the wage.

front: The least-cost rule: equal marginal product per dollar for every input.
cue: Choosing the input mix that makes an output at least cost.
worked: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>20</mn><mrow><mo>$</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{20}{$10}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext> units per dollar</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 2\,\text{ units per dollar}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Use each input's own price, and compare products per dollar, not marginal utility.

cue: A monopsony or any hiring answer.
trap: A monopsonist pays the wage read from labor supply at the number hired.
